seoTitle: Case Study: Auto Dealership Group Catalytic Converter Theft
metaDescription: A Southeast auto dealer group eliminated catalytic converter theft across 7 lots in 90 days with Swift Deploy and LPR integration
h1: Seven lots, four catalytic converter thefts per month, zero in 90 days
heroSubhead: A Southeast dealer group deployed Swift Deploy with LPR integration across seven new and used lots. Pre-deployment baseline: an average of four catalytic converter thefts per month. Ninety days post-deployment: zero. Annual avoided loss: $128,000.
body:
## Customer profile

A privately held automotive dealer group operating seven retail lots across two Southeast metro markets. The group sells four franchised new-vehicle brands plus a centralized used-vehicle operation. Combined nightly inventory exposure: approximately 1,400 vehicles. The group requested anonymization for competitive reasons.

## The problem

For the 18 months prior to engagement, the dealer group averaged 4.1 catalytic converter thefts per month across the seven lots — concentrated heavily on hybrid and pickup inventory parked on outer-perimeter rows. Average per-incident cost: $2,600 (replacement converter, labor, paint touch-up where the underbody saw exposure, customer-loaner expense when a sold unit was found cut before delivery). Annualized exposure: approximately $128,000 in direct replacement cost, plus a harder-to-quantify reputational cost when buyers found out a unit on the lot had been cut.

The group's existing security posture consisted of standard fixed dome cameras recording to a local DVR, motion-activated floodlights, and an overnight alarm-monitored intrusion system that triggered on the showroom doors only. None of these systems had produced a single successful intervention against the converter theft pattern, because the cuts were happening 80+ feet from the showroom in 90 seconds or less.

The general manager evaluated three options: hire overnight security guards across the seven lots (estimated $610,000/year), install perimeter fencing and gated lots (estimated $340,000 capex, would conflict with the brand's franchise display standards), or deploy mobile surveillance with LPR and live monitoring.

## The configuration

VDS deployed Swift Deploy units configured for dealer lot use, with the following adaptations:

- **One Swift Deploy per lot at the highest-loss two lots; shared coverage at the remaining five lots via three units rotating on a two-week reposition cycle.**
- **LPR integration:** Every vehicle entering and leaving the lot during after-hours had its plate captured, timestamped, and logged to the Cloud VMS. The SOC was given a hot-list of known regional theft-crew plates supplied by local LE intelligence units.
- **Thermal-mode evening hours:** From 9pm to 5am, units ran in thermal-priority mode to identify human heat signatures crossing the perimeter regardless of light conditions.
- **Audio talk-down:** Enabled at every unit with a dealer-specific script tied to the group's preferred LE coordination protocol.

The VDS SOC monitored all units 24/7. The dealer group's IT team integrated the VMS event feed into the group's existing incident-tracking tool, and the GM received a weekly summary email.

## The first 30 days

Within the first week, the SOC issued nine audio talk-downs across the seven lots. Two of those involved subjects on hands and knees beside vehicles with reciprocating saws visible. Both subjects fled on first audio contact. LE was dispatched on both events and recovered tools and partial converter inventory from a vehicle the suspects abandoned a block away.

By week three, the LPR hot-list had flagged the same vehicle plate at two different lots on two different nights. That plate was supplied to LE, who linked it to a multi-county theft ring that was indicted four months later in a federal case unrelated to this customer's loss but informed in part by the LPR data the SOC had captured.

## The 90-day outcome

Across the 90-day measurement window:

- **Catalytic converter thefts:** Zero (down from an expected 12 across that window based on baseline rate).
- **Direct avoided loss:** $31,000 over the 90-day window; annualized: $128,000.
- **Audio talk-downs:** 41 across the seven lots.
- **LE dispatches:** 6. Three resulted in arrests directly tied to this customer's lots. One additional LPR record contributed to a regional theft-ring indictment.
- **False alarm rate:** Under 4% of SOC-reviewed events. Slightly higher than the platform average due to legitimate after-hours porter traffic until the SOC tuned the schedule whitelist.
- **Insurance carrier response:** The group's commercial auto inventory policy was reviewed at next renewal with no rate increase, and the carrier requested a copy of the deployment configuration as a reference for other dealer clients.

## What the customer said

The GM at the highest-loss lot summarized the deployment at the 90-day review: "We had spent two years buying alarms that called us after the fact. The Swift Deploy talks back before the saw comes out."

## Configuration notes for other dealer groups

Two adjustments we now recommend by default for dealer lot deployments. First, run units in thermal-priority mode after 9pm rather than relying solely on visible-light. Catalytic converter theft is almost always a ground-level activity in low-light conditions, and thermal is decisive. Second, integrate LPR with whatever local LE intelligence unit will accept a hot-list feed. The deterrent value of a known plate getting flagged is significant beyond the individual customer.

metaDescription: A $28M Mid-Atlantic general contractor cut jobsite theft 73% and saved $340,800 in 12 months with two Swift Deploy units and three Solar Camera Poles
h1: How a $28M Mid-Atlantic GC cut jobsite theft 73% and saved $340,800
heroSubhead: Two Swift Deploy units, three Solar Camera Poles, 24/7 US SOC monitoring. Twelve months of verified data: 73% reduction in theft incidents, $0 in insurance claims, $340,800 in avoided loss.
body:
## Customer profile

A general contracting firm headquartered in the Mid-Atlantic, $28M in annual revenue, running three concurrent commercial construction projects ranging from a mixed-use mid-rise to a regional distribution center. Combined active jobsite footprint: approximately 14 acres. The firm self-performs concrete, structural steel coordination, and MEP rough-in oversight.

## The problem

Across the prior 18 months, the GC absorbed an average of $42,500 per month in direct theft loss: copper wire pulls from staged conduit runs, three stolen 5500-watt portable generators, two skid steers (one recovered, one written off), small tools and fuel from gang boxes, and a recurring pattern of late-night perimeter breaches that triggered insurance scrutiny. The firm's commercial insurance carrier flagged the loss ratio and signaled that the next renewal would either include a theft exclusion or a premium increase the principal estimated at $60,000 to $90,000 annually.

The CFO and the firm's risk manager evaluated three alternatives: hire two overnight guards per active site (estimated $312,000/year per site for two 12-hour posts), install trenched conduit and pole-mounted IP cameras at each site (estimated $85,000 capex per site, six-week deployment, abandoned at project close), or deploy mobile surveillance with live monitoring.

## The configuration

VDS deployed two Swift Deploy mobile surveillance trailers and three Solar Camera Poles across the three active sites. Deployment summary:

- **Site A (mid-rise, 4.5 acres):** One Swift Deploy at the primary site entrance covering the material lay-down yard. Two Solar Camera Poles at the rear perimeter where the access road met an adjacent commercial property.
- **Site B (distribution center pad, 6.2 acres):** One Swift Deploy at the southwest corner covering the generator and fuel storage area. One Solar Camera Pole at the northeast corner covering staged copper and electrical materials.
- **Site C (interior renovation, 3.1 acres):** Coverage shared with Site B via repositioning between phases; no permanent unit on this site after week 6.

All units fed into the VDS Cloud VMS, with 24/7 monitoring by the US-based SOC. Audio talk-down enabled at every unit. Local LE coordination established with the township police departments serving each site in week one.

## The first 30 days

Within the first ten days, the SOC issued 14 audio talk-downs. Eleven resulted in immediate departure of the subject. Three escalated to LE dispatch — average response time 11 minutes, two arrests on Site A for trespass and attempted larceny. By day 30, the foot-traffic pattern at all three sites had measurably shifted: the SOC was logging an average of 0.8 perimeter approaches per night across the portfolio, down from a pre-deployment baseline the firm's own night-shift superintendent estimated at 4 to 6.

## The 12-month outcome

Across the measurement year:

- **Theft incidents:** 8 (down from a baseline of 29 in the prior comparable window) — a 73% reduction.
- **Direct theft loss:** $14,200 (down from a baseline of approximately $355,000) — $340,800 in avoided loss.
- **Insurance claims filed:** Zero. The renewal came back with the prior premium and no exclusion.
- **SOC audio talk-downs:** 187 across the portfolio.
- **LE dispatches:** 9. Five resulted in arrests, four were clear-on-arrival.
- **False alarm rate:** Under 3% of all SOC-reviewed events, consistent with the platform's documented 97% false alarm reduction.
- **Downtime:** Zero. Solar-autonomous units sustained continuous operation through two ice events and one named tropical storm.

## What the customer said

The firm's risk manager summarized the deployment in a single line during the contract renewal call: "We spent under $90,000 to avoid $340,000 in loss and an insurance fight we were going to lose. The math is not complicated."

## What we would do differently

In retrospect, Site C did not require its own unit. The repositioning model we adopted in week six produced equivalent coverage and reduced the customer's monthly spend. We now recommend this approach by default on portfolios with three or more small concurrent sites and adjacent access.

h1: Three substations, six copper thefts, then nine months at zero
heroSubhead: A Mid-Atlantic electric utility deployed Sky Guard MSU at three substation perimeters after a six-month run of copper theft. Nine months later: zero incidents, $180,000 in copper protected, $42,000 in avoided LE callout fees.
body:
## Customer profile

A regional electric distribution utility operating in the Mid-Atlantic with approximately 240,000 metered customers. The customer requested anonymization for security and regulatory reasons. The three substations covered in this case study are distribution-level (not transmission), located in suburban-to-exurban areas with limited natural surveillance and adjacent right-of-way access.

## The problem

Across a six-month window, the utility experienced six confirmed copper theft incidents at three substations. The pattern was consistent: late-night perimeter breach through fence-cutting, theft of grounding conductor, ground-grid jumpers, and in one incident the copper bushings off a de-energized transformer staged for replacement. The direct material replacement cost per incident averaged $14,000 to $38,000, but the larger operational exposure was the safety risk to first responders and the regulatory scrutiny from the state PUC tied to repeated perimeter compromise events.

Total measured exposure across the six-month window: approximately $138,000 in replaced copper, $26,000 in emergency repair labor, $18,000 in LE callout and incident-response fees (the township billed for repeated after-hours calls), and an unquantified but material regulatory liability under NERC CIP-014 reporting thresholds for physical security incidents at distribution facilities adjacent to load-pocket transmission.

The utility evaluated three options: install fixed IP camera systems with on-site recording (estimated $145,000 per substation, 14-week procurement and install cycle, no live monitoring), contract local guard services ($186,000/year per substation for overnight coverage), or deploy mobile surveillance with 24/7 monitoring.

## The configuration

VDS deployed one Sky Guard MSU at each of the three substations. Sky Guard was selected over Swift Deploy because the substations required permanent multi-year coverage rather than redeployable mobility, and because the unit's extended-runtime solar profile fit the utility's preference for zero grid dependency on the surveillance system itself. Each unit was positioned at the corner of the substation fence line with the longest sight lines to the fence perimeter and the staged equipment areas.

All units fed into the VDS Cloud VMS. The utility's own physical security operations center maintained a viewer credential for situational awareness, but live monitoring and dispatch coordination ran through the VDS SOC. Audio talk-down was enabled at every unit. Two-stage escalation was configured: SOC operator verification within 30 seconds, audio talk-down within 60 seconds for verified intrusions, simultaneous LE dispatch and utility security duty officer notification for any verified perimeter breach.

NDAA Section 889 compliance was a procurement requirement. All hardware deployed met that standard.

## The first 60 days

Within the first three weeks, the SOC issued 22 audio talk-downs across the three sites. Nine of those involved subjects actively scaling or cutting the fence. Seven resulted in immediate departure. Two escalated to LE dispatch with arrests. The utility's security duty officer received four after-hours notifications, all confirmed as legitimate threats rather than false alarms — a sharp contrast with the prior fixed-alarm system that had generated an average of 2.4 false alarms per night across the three sites.

By day 60, the SOC was logging fewer than three approach events per week across the entire three-site portfolio.

## The 9-month outcome

Across the nine-month measurement window:

- **Confirmed copper theft incidents:** Zero (down from six in the prior comparable window).
- **Material protected (estimated value at risk):** $180,000 — calculated from the average per-incident loss in the pre-deployment window multiplied by the expected incident rate.
- **LE callout fees avoided:** $42,000 — the township's billed rate for after-hours response calls. The utility shifted from an average of 1.1 LE callouts per month to 0.3.
- **False alarm rate:** Under 2% of all SOC-reviewed events.
- **Audio talk-downs:** 58 across the portfolio.
- **LE dispatches with arrests:** 4.
- **System downtime:** Zero. All three units sustained operation through two named winter storms and a three-day regional grid outage that affected the substations themselves — the surveillance kept running on solar and battery while the substations were de-energized.

## What the customer said

The utility's physical security manager noted in the renewal review: "The substations stayed dark for 72 hours and the cameras did not. That is the headline."

## NERC CIP and reporting

The utility uses the VDS Cloud VMS audit log as a contributing data source for physical security incident reporting. Every event is timestamped, every SOC operator action is logged, and every retention policy is configurable to meet the utility's record-keeping requirements. The platform was reviewed by the utility's compliance team prior to deployment.
